newsitem.title: USA: IBM CEO to address mostly happier investors.
newsitem.headline: IBM CEO to address mostly happier investors.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp Chairman and CEO Louis Gerstner will address his fourth annual meeting Tuesday and shareholders -- while pleased with the rebound in the stock price -- are also expected to grill the CEO on the computer giant's seemingly paltry dividend.

Analysts said IBM could announce another slight uptick in its dividend payout before the meeting begins in Dallas, but they said it is more likely IBM will continue its current path of buying back stock with another buyback plan.

"They might increase their share authorization," said David Takata, a Gruntal & Co analyst. "They only have $800 milion left in the current plan," he said referring to IBM's latest share buyback plan it announced last November.

In the first quarter, IBM spent about $2 billion buying back its stock, under its current authorization plan, reducing the number of its shares outstanding to 501.7 million, from 544.3 million a year ago.

Analysts said that buying back stock is a better use of IBM's cash pile, which was $6.4 billion at the end of the first quarter, than a dividend. A hefty dividend payment can lock up part of IBM's cash and also sets the stage for it to be lowered during downturns in business.
"For years, they were borrowing to pay it," said Gary Helmig, a SoundView Financial Group analyst. "The dividend is a treadmill."

When financial woes beset the behemoth in the early 1990s, IBM's peak annual dividend payout was $4.84 a share. Amid huge losses, layoffs and an unprecedented CEO search, IBM also slashed its dividend for the first time in its corporate history in January 1993.

Now IBM's annual dividend is $1.40 a share, after an increase at last year's meeting from $1.00 a year. The level is respectable for a technology company, as most technology firms do not pay dividends and reinvest their cash in research and development. But for IBM shareholders it is relatively thin.

Since IBM's cash position is improving as it generates funds almost every quarter from operations, shareholders want more returns. But analysts also point out that IBM stock buybacks ultimately help boost its share price.

In its first quarter earnings, IBM was able to surpass most Wall Street estimates despite a decline in mainframes, minicomputers and workstation sales. It was helped by a lower tax rate, fewer shares outstanding and revenue growth in other faster growing, but lower margin businesses. Its shares soared $11.25 to $153.625 on Thursday, following its late Wednesday earnings report.
On Friday, profit-taking hit the stock, which fell 2-7/8 to close at $150-3/4.

During IBM's conference call with analysts late Thursday, one analyst queried Chief Financial Officer G. Richard Thoman on the dividend, noting his poor widowed mother is a long-term investor who used to rely on the IBM payout as part of her income.

"Well, there is Philip Morris," Thoman joked. "We do a lot of thinking about what's right for our investors and we think the share buyback program is part of our future." But he declined to predict what IBM's next move would be in buying back shares, or on possibly raising the dividend.

Gerstner, who joined IBM after its first-ever CEO search in April 1993, is expected to tout IBM's improved financials and its stock price, which approached its all-time high of $175-3/4 in January when it hit $170-1/8, but fell back to the $130 range on concerns about its single-digit revenue growth.

Shareholders may also focus on its low price/earnings ratio of about 11.4 times 1997 earnings estimates, which many bullish analysts on IBM say represents a buying opportunity. Some Wall Street targets on IBM stock are in the $178-185 range.
